entries.title: Guitar Hero II
entries.subtitle: Two guitars, shared songs and a place to practise the solo
entries.summary: Harmonix expanded Guitar Hero with cooperative lead and bass or rhythm parts, and a practice mode for difficult passages.
story_headings: A second guitar joins the stage
body: Released first for PlayStation 2 on November 7, 2006, Guitar Hero II kept the pleasure of turning a familiar riff into a physical sequence of fretting and strumming. Harmonix added cooperative play: one player takes the lead guitar while another follows the bass or rhythm part. The original PlayStation 2 selection contains 64 songs, combining licensed rock songs, many newly recorded as covers, with bonus tracks. The Xbox 360 edition followed in April 2007 with additional material and an X-Plorer controller.

Practice mode makes repetition part of the game rather than a punishment for failure. A player can isolate a section, slow it down and work towards playing it at full speed. Improved hammer-ons and pull-offs make flowing phrases more comfortable, while three-note chords add another demand. The plastic instrument does not teach the exact fingering of a real guitar; it turns listening, coordination and remembering a musical phrase into a visible, repeatable challenge.

entries.title: Guitar Hero III: Legends of Rock
entries.subtitle: Neversoft turns the guitar duel into a rock spectacle
entries.summary: The first Neversoft Guitar Hero mixed familiar note highways with a cooperative career, online competition and battles against guitar icons.
story_headings: A new studio takes the stage
Turning a solo into a duel
body: Guitar Hero III: Legends of Rock launched in North America on October 28, 2007. Neversoft took over the principal development role after Harmonix’s earlier games; other studios handled particular versions. The game kept the five-colour note highway and guitar-controller performance while building a career around increasingly demanding venues and songs. Its 73 playable songs mix original recordings and covers. A separate cooperative career gives two players lead and bass or rhythm parts, while several console versions also offered online competition.

The new Battle mode lets opponents disrupt one another rather than simply compare scores. Special note sequences award attacks that can interfere with the other player’s instrument or performance, making familiar musical patterns suddenly harder to read. Slash and Tom Morello appear as opponents, linking the plastic-guitar fantasy to recognisable performers. These theatrical confrontations sit alongside the more direct satisfaction of following a riff accurately, maintaining a streak and finally surviving a difficult solo.

entries.title: Rock Band
entries.subtitle: Four different parts become one performance
entries.summary: Harmonix broadened the plastic-guitar phenomenon into a shared performance for guitar, bass, drums and vocals.
body: Rock Band first reached North American PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 players on November 20, 2007. Developed by Harmonix, published by MTV Games and distributed by Electronic Arts, it expanded the musical-controller idea beyond the guitar. Up to four people follow separate guitar, bass, drum and vocal parts within the same song. The original disc contains 58 tracks, including established rock artists and bonus songs from smaller acts. PlayStation 2 and Wii editions followed, with differences in their tour features and downloadable-content support.

A band shares its score, but each player can choose a different difficulty. Guitarists watch note lanes, the drummer follows pads and a pedal, and the singer matches pitch against a vocal line. Overdrive adds a collective decision: its energy can raise the score or help bring a failed band member back into the song. The result is more than four independent score attacks. An experienced player can support a newcomer, and a familiar recording becomes a small exercise in listening and cooperation.

entries.title: The Beatles: Rock Band
entries.subtitle: The Beatles’ musical history becomes a performance to share
entries.summary: Harmonix built a dedicated Beatles game around the band’s recordings, historic venues, three-part vocal harmonies and imaginative studio dreamscapes.
story_headings: From the Cavern Club to the rooftop
body: Released worldwide on September 9, 2009 for PlayStation 3, Xbox 360 and Wii, The Beatles: Rock Band follows the group through 45 songs on the original disc. Harmonix developed the game with Apple Corps’ involvement, with MTV Games publishing and Electronic Arts distributing it. The story moves through recognisable moments and places in the band’s career, including the Cavern Club, the Ed Sullivan Show, Shea Stadium, Budokan and the Apple rooftop. Costumes, instruments and performances change with the period.

The familiar guitar, bass and drum parts are joined by support for three-part vocal harmonies. Up to six people can perform together when three singers join the instrumental players. Singing is not simply another coloured lane: several voices can follow distinct pitches at the same time. Training modes let players practise those relationships. The game also avoids some of the intrusive sounds used elsewhere in Rock Band, allowing the Beatles’ recordings to remain at the centre of the experience.

For the studio years, the band moves from Abbey Road into animated dreamscapes inspired by the songs. These are artistic interpretations rather than reconstructions of concerts that never happened. Giles Martin served as music producer, helping adapt the original recordings for an interactive mix. Additional Beatles songs and albums were later offered as downloadable content, separate from the original 45-song disc selection. The dedicated game remains a distinct interpretation of the band’s work, rather than a general Rock Band expansion.

entries.title: Guitar Hero World Tour
entries.subtitle: Guitar Hero makes room for the whole band
entries.summary: World Tour added drums, vocals and a music studio to the series’ guitar-and-bass performance.
body: Guitar Hero World Tour arrived in North America on October 26, 2008, bringing drums and vocals into the main Guitar Hero series alongside lead guitar and bass. Neversoft led development, with other studios responsible for particular versions. Its 86-song disc selection uses master recordings, and four players can build a band around different musical roles. The new drum controller adds raised cymbal pads, while a revised guitar introduces a touch-sensitive section for particular passages.

Music Studio offers a different relationship with the instrument controllers: players can construct instrumental songs rather than only follow an existing recording. The accompanying GHTunes service originally allowed those creations to be shared. The studio does not turn the peripherals into ordinary acoustic instruments; it gives their gestures a creative use within the game’s own musical system. Character, instrument and band customisation extend that idea of putting together a performance of one’s own.

entries.title: Guitar Hero 5
entries.subtitle: The band line-up becomes a choice rather than a rule
entries.summary: Guitar Hero 5 emphasised flexible instrument combinations and uninterrupted Party Play, with every disc song available from the start.
story_headings: A band on your own terms
Let the next player join in
body: Released first in North America on September 1, 2009, Guitar Hero 5 kept the full-band format while loosening its rules. Up to four players can choose any combination of guitar, bass, drums and vocals, including several copies of the same instrument. The disc contains 85 songs by 83 artists, all available immediately in Quickplay. Neversoft’s design makes the group’s preferred roles more important than filling a prescribed band line-up.

Party Play lets people enter or leave without stopping the current song, turning the game into something that can remain running during a gathering. Career mode adds instrument-specific challenges, giving familiar tracks another purpose beyond simply finishing them. The game also retained a music studio and supported compatible earlier downloadable songs. Those libraries and services belong to the game’s historical context; their original presence is distinct from what remains available through later online services.

entries.title: Guitar Hero: Warriors of Rock
entries.subtitle: A rock setlist becomes a fantasy quest
entries.summary: Warriors of Rock wrapped the band format in a narrated quest, transforming its musicians into characters with different gameplay powers.
story_headings: A story told through the setlist
body: Guitar Hero: Warriors of Rock appeared in September 2010 for PlayStation 3, Xbox 360 and Wii. Its Quest mode, narrated by Gene Simmons, recruits eight musicians whose transformed forms grant different powers. The guitar, bass, drum and vocal parts remain the foundation, but character abilities alter scoring and how players survive songs. The 93-song disc selection leans towards rock and metal, giving the fantasy campaign a musical identity rather than abandoning the band format.

Rush’s seven-part 2112 becomes a sustained chapter of the journey, while Megadeth’s Sudden Death was created for the game’s culmination. Outside the story, Quickplay+ adds challenges to individual tracks, and flexible band combinations carry forward ideas from Guitar Hero 5. This was Neversoft’s last Guitar Hero. Its elaborate quest marks a particular response to the rhythm-game boom: make the familiar act of following notes feel like a theatrical adventure.

entries.title: Guitar Hero Live
entries.subtitle: A different guitar, and a crowd that looks back
entries.summary: FreeStyleGames rebooted Guitar Hero with a two-row controller and concert footage filmed from the guitarist’s point of view.
story_headings: A concert and a music-video channel
body: Guitar Hero Live launched in North America on October 20, 2015. FreeStyleGames replaced the earlier five-colour guitar with six fret buttons arranged in two rows of three. Its patterns ask the fretting hand to move between rows as well as along the neck. The Live mode places the note highway over filmed concerts seen from the lead guitarist’s perspective, with the crowd and fellow musicians reacting to how well the player performs.

The original release separated the 42-song Live selection from GHTV, an online network of playable music videos. Instead of owning those streamed tracks as conventional downloadable songs, players joined programmed channels or spent in-game resources on plays. The distinction became important when GHTV closed on December 1, 2018: its network catalogue was separate from the on-disc Live performances. The new controller and filmed stage presentation make this a deliberate reinvention, not another edition of the earlier five-fret games.

entries.title: Rock Band 2
entries.subtitle: The shared tour becomes a platform for a growing music library
entries.summary: Rock Band 2 developed the original band format with an online World Tour, drum training and a new disc selection built from master recordings.
body: Rock Band 2 first appeared on Xbox 360 in North America on September 14, 2008, with PlayStation 3, PlayStation 2 and Wii versions following later. Harmonix retained guitar, bass, drums and vocals for up to four players. Its 84-song disc selection uses master recordings rather than newly commissioned cover performances. Compatible downloadable music and an authorised export of much of the first game’s disc helped make the sequel feel like an expanding library, not an isolated setlist.

World Tour extended the band’s journey into online play, while challenges offered other routes through the repertoire. Drum Trainer separated rhythmic patterns and fills from the pressure of a complete song, making the drum controller a place to practise as well as perform. A No Fail option made mixed-skill gatherings more welcoming. The refinements concentrate on continuity: keep the group playing, accommodate different abilities and let a familiar collection of songs acquire new uses.

entries.title: Rock Band 4
entries.subtitle: The band returns to a new console generation
entries.summary: Harmonix brought guitar, bass, drums and vocals to PlayStation 4 and Xbox One, placing shared performance and musical improvisation at the centre.
body: Rock Band 4 launched for PlayStation 4 and Xbox One on October 6, 2015. Harmonix developed and published the game, with Mad Catz initially handling distribution and new instrument controllers. Its 65-song core soundtrack accompanied a renewed emphasis on guitar, bass, drums and vocals. The move to new consoles also involved bringing forward eligible purchases from earlier music libraries, subject to platform and licensing conditions. This is the original 2015 game, not the later Rivals expansion.

Freestyle guitar solos and freer vocal melodies let players add some expression rather than reproduce every displayed note literally. The band can also keep a session moving by voting on what to play next. Rock Band 4 leaves behind Rock Band 3’s keyboard and Pro guitar focus, concentrating instead on the social performance of a familiar band. Its historical importance lies in continuity: a new console generation became another stage for songs, instruments and friendships accumulated over earlier games.

entries.title: Guitar Hero Encore: Rocks the 80s
entries.subtitle: The last Harmonix encore
entries.summary: A PlayStation 2 encore turns Guitar Hero II’s familiar stage into a celebration of eighties rock.
story_headings: An encore rather than a reinvention
body: Released for PlayStation 2 in 2007, Guitar Hero Encore: Rocks the 80s concentrates its repertoire into thirty songs. New wave, hard rock and heavy metal share the same scrolling note highway, with familiar characters and venues dressed for the decade. Most recordings are covers, alongside a smaller group of artist recordings; even those require care when comparing editions, since the game’s I Wanna Rock uses a re-recording rather than the original album performance.

The playing system closely follows Guitar Hero II: matching frets and strums keeps a performance alive, while Star Power can turn a carefully chosen phrase into a larger score. The attraction is a fresh repertoire rather than a new instrument or a full-band format. Its relatively small selection and limited mechanical changes divided reviewers. It was also Harmonix’s last Guitar Hero release before the studio moved on to Rock Band.

entries.title: Guitar Hero: Aerosmith
entries.subtitle: A career told through the setlist
entries.summary: Aerosmith’s music, venues and digital band members turn Guitar Hero into a playable band retrospective.
body: Guitar Hero: Aerosmith makes one band the organising principle of an entire game. Its career moves through six tiers associated with stages in Aerosmith’s history. Songs by opening acts introduce each section before the player takes on the band’s own repertoire. The underlying guitar play comes from Guitar Hero III, with fret patterns, strumming and Star Power, rather than the four-instrument ensemble introduced by World Tour.

The band contributed motion capture so that its members could appear as recognisable performers on the virtual stage. The soundtrack combines Aerosmith recordings with music by other acts, and several early Aerosmith songs were re-recorded for the project. Venues and contextual material make the career more than a list of unrelated challenges, although reviewers also questioned the shorter, generally easier selection. The original console release was followed by a computer edition later in 2008.

entries.title: Guitar Hero: Metallica
entries.subtitle: The whole band, at full force
entries.summary: Metallica’s repertoire brings guitars, drums and vocals together, with a demanding new double-bass challenge.
body: Guitar Hero: Metallica builds on World Tour’s four-player band format, supporting lead guitar, bass, drums and vocals. Metallica’s songs sit alongside pieces by other artists selected for the game, turning the setlist into both a portrait of the band and a broader hard-rock conversation. The group’s members contributed motion capture, and the venues draw on its imagery, album themes and live identity.

The drum part received particular attention. Expert+ adds double-bass patterns for players using a second kick pedal, while practice tools help break difficult passages into manageable sections. Guitar, bass and vocal players still take part in the same shared performance rather than a separate drum-only game. Alongside career progression, the game retained competitive and music-creation features derived from World Tour, with Metallica-specific instrument sounds and presentation.

entries.title: Lego Rock Band
entries.subtitle: Build a band and rock the universe
entries.summary: Plastic instruments meet minifigures in a musical adventure that turns successful performances into bricks, vehicles and improbable gigs.
story_headings: A gentler way onto the stage
body: Lego Rock Band joins the four-player instrument performances of Rock Band to LEGO’s customisable minifigures and comic storytelling. Guitar, bass, drums and vocals still follow their own musical parts, but the tour can carry the band from ordinary gigs into fantastical situations. Successful playing earns studs, which help furnish a rock den and develop the band’s identity. Rock Power Challenges make the performance itself the answer to a spectacular problem, such as bringing down a building.

The console repertoire contains forty-five songs chosen for a family audience. A Super Easy setting and other accessibility options make it easier for newcomers to participate without mastering every note. The Nintendo DS edition is a different handheld design: one player switches between instruments, and its selection contains twenty-five songs rather than the complete console repertoire. The original release also offered selected family-appropriate downloadable music on supported consoles; that historical service should not be confused with a promise of present-day availability.

entries.title: Rock Band Unplugged
entries.subtitle: An entire band in your hands
entries.summary: Rock Band returns to Harmonix’s lane-switching roots, making one PSP player responsible for every part of a song.
body: Rock Band Unplugged replaces the living-room collection of plastic instruments with the PSP itself. One player moves between guitar, bass, drum and vocal lanes, completing phrases that let an instrument continue playing automatically for a while. The challenge is not simply to finish one part: attention has to circulate through the whole band before unattended instruments begin to fail. The design recalls Harmonix’s Frequency and Amplitude while retaining Rock Band’s familiar musical presentation.

The original game includes forty-one master recordings and a customisable touring band. World Tour carries the musicians through venues and sets, while Band Survival and Warmup offer different ways to approach the note patterns. Overdrive provides a familiar link with the console series. The full retail game is distinct from the later downloadable Unplugged Lite edition, which began with a smaller starter selection; the original PSP release also supported an in-game music store, a feature of its historical launch rather than a guarantee that songs remain on sale.

entries.title: Rock Band Blitz
entries.subtitle: The band becomes an arcade machine
entries.summary: Five musical lanes, a standard controller and an appetite for points turn Rock Band into a fast single-player score chase.
body: Rock Band Blitz dispenses with instrument peripherals and places one player in charge of as many as five musical lanes. Rather than settling into a single instrumental role, the player switches lanes to build their multipliers and keep the whole arrangement productive. Successful stretches trigger Blitz mode, accelerating the spectacle and the opportunities to score. The result is deliberately arcade-like: a song becomes a shifting field of decisions rather than a simulation of standing in a band.

Different power-ups add another layer of planning, turning selected notes or moments into opportunities for a larger score. The original release included twenty-five songs, and it could also adapt compatible music from the wider Rock Band library. Its own songs were playable in Rock Band 3 as well. Blitz first arrived on PlayStation Network in August 2012, followed by Xbox Live Arcade the next day; it was removed from sale in 2017 when music licences expired.

entries.title: Guitar Hero: Van Halen
entries.subtitle: One band, four instruments
entries.summary: Van Halen’s early repertoire becomes a full-band rhythm game, with Eddie’s guitar solos at its centre.
story_headings: Four parts on the same stage
body: Guitar Hero: Van Halen brings lead guitar, bass, drums and vocals to the band’s repertoire. Twenty-five Van Halen songs and three Eddie Van Halen guitar solos appear alongside nineteen songs by other artists. The selection concentrates on the David Lee Roth era rather than covering every period of the group. The playable band reflects the 2009 line-up, including Wolfgang Van Halen; earlier appearances can be unlocked, but former members are not playable.

Developed by Underground Development, the game follows the full-band approach of World Tour and Metallica rather than the newer Party Play features of Guitar Hero 5. Eddie’s solos provide demanding guitar challenges, while the other instruments support a shared performance. North American purchasers of Guitar Hero 5 could receive the game through an early promotion before its retail release on December 22, 2009. The timeline date refers to that retail release, not the first promotional deliveries.

entries.title: Band Hero
entries.subtitle: The living room becomes a pop stage
entries.summary: A pop-oriented sibling to Guitar Hero 5 opens the band format to familiar radio hits and flexible instrument combinations.
story_headings: A band that fits in your hands
body: Band Hero shifts the emphasis from guitar-led rock towards a broader pop repertoire. The console versions offer sixty-five songs and adopt Guitar Hero 5’s flexible band format: players can join a performance, change difficulty and combine instruments freely. Taylor Swift, Adam Levine and No Doubt appear as performers. The PlayStation 2 version uses the older World Tour engine, so the newer consoles’ features should not be assumed to be identical on every platform.

The Nintendo DS edition is a distinct handheld adaptation with thirty songs. Guitar and bass use the Guitar Grip, which requires a Game Boy Advance cartridge slot. A drum skin fitted to the DS Lite maps percussion to its buttons, while the microphone handles singing. These physical requirements matter: the full accessory-based ensemble belongs to the DS Lite, not to every DS model. The handheld game illustrates how one musical idea could demand very different controls.

entries.title: AC/DC Live: Rock Band Track Pack
entries.subtitle: A concert becomes the setlist
entries.summary: Eighteen live performances from Donington become a standalone Rock Band game for guitar, bass, drums and vocals.
story_headings: A complete disc, with fewer extras
body: AC/DC Live: Rock Band Track Pack turns the band’s 1991 Donington concert repertoire into eighteen playable live recordings. Guitar, bass, drums and vocals follow the familiar Rock Band format, but the audible crowd and the band’s live phrasing give this selection a different character from a collection of studio singles. It is a standalone game: an existing Rock Band disc is not required to play it with compatible instruments.

The North American PlayStation 2, PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 editions arrived on November 2, 2008; Wii followed later that month. The disc omits several features of the main games, including character customisation and online play. Its original PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 editions included a code to export the songs into compatible Rock Band games. That was a release-era offer, not a promise that old codes or export services remain available today.
